articles.title: How We Built a True Client-Side PDF Redaction Engine in the Browser
articles.excerpt: When users need to redact sensitive data from a PDF—such as tax returns, medical records, or legal contracts—they often rely on online web utilities. However, most free PDF redact tools on the web per…
articles.body: When users need to redact sensitive data from a PDF—such as tax returns, medical records, or legal contracts—they often rely on online web utilities. However, most free PDF redact tools on the web perform visual masking , simply drawing a black rectangle ( #000000 ) over the existing text object. This is a massive security risk: the underlying vector text and streams remain fully preserved in the file's binary object stream, allowing anyone to open the PDF, highlight the text under the black box, and copy it out. To solve this, we built a zero-upload PDF Redaction Engine using WebAssembly, HTML5 Canvas, and pdf-lib . Here is how it permanently strips text objects and burns redactions into document streams directly inside the browser. The Architecture: Visual Masking vs.

articles.title: A Practical Python Checklist for Automating Repetitive Work
articles.excerpt: Python automation works best when it removes a repeatable step without making the process harder to trust. Before writing a script, define the input, output, rules, and what should happen when somethi…
articles.body: Python automation works best when it removes a repeatable step without making the process harder to trust. Before writing a script, define the input, output, rules, and what should happen when something is missing. Start with a one-sentence specification Write down the job in this form: “Given this input , produce this output , using these rules , and stop or report when this condition occurs.” If those details are still changing, clarify the process before automating it. For example, a monthly contact export might need consistent names and email addresses. That is a good candidate for a small Python script if the file format and rules are stable. A workflow that includes judgment, approvals, or exceptions may need a human review step instead of full automation.

articles.body: OBI Robotics × Ontological Bayesian Intelligence 12-week engineering roadmap OBINexus Computing · Mechanical-first development · C/C++ robotics · 20 hours per week The objective is to turn OBI Robotics from an architecture and CAD concept into a testable physical prototype, while developing the Ontological Bayesian Intelligence (OBI) as a separate, measurable reasoning system that can eventually operate with the robot. The engineering principle: design the physical system first, model what it can sense and do, then build intelligence around the actual constraints of that system. Your uploaded Unbiased_AI.pdf provides the proposed intelligence framework: Bayesian modelling for bias analysis, structural processing, modular AI components and a staged implementation roadmap.

articles.title: Rethinking the LLM Knowledge Base: Maybe Just Start with an LLM Wiki?
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: GraphRAG and LLM Wiki both "distill" raw data with an LLM, and they hit similar problems: wrong summaries, stale knowledge, lost sources, and hard evaluation. I could not find a clear answer on…
articles.body: TL;DR : GraphRAG and LLM Wiki both "distill" raw data with an LLM, and they hit similar problems: wrong summaries, stale knowledge, lost sources, and hard evaluation. I could not find a clear answer on how thick the distilled layer should be. If you start small, I would go with an LLM Wiki. I needed to figure out how to build a knowledge base that keeps growing, so I looked into it again and tried to sort things out. I searched widely for existing products, the main methods, and recent papers, and then deepened my understanding by talking with an AI. When I think of LLM knowledge bases, I think of two families: GraphRAG and LLM Wiki. I dug into both and found that they have more in common than I expected, so I am leaving these notes.

articles.body: TL;DR Most WooCommerce stores publish their full catalog publicly, including prices, sale prices, SKUs and stock, so a competitor's catalog can be monitored without logins, plugins or page-by-page scraping . The useful part is diffing : snapshot the catalog on a schedule and send only what changed (new, removed, price changed, stock changed) to Slack, email or Sheets. In three real stores we checked on Oct 20, 2026, 13–36% of products were out of stock and 1–15% were on sale . Those are the fields that move day to day. A daily check of a 1,000-product competitor with 10 changes costs about $0.25 a run with our monitor actor. The first (baseline) run is never charged for changes. articles.title: Google Chrome is done warning you about insecure websites after the fact
articles.excerpt: The browser will now give you a heads-up before you visit an insecure website.
articles.body: TL;DR Google is enabling Chrome’s “Always Use Secure Connections” setting for all users by default. Chrome will now warn users before connecting to insecure HTTP websites, giving them a chance to back out. Chrome won’t repeatedly warn users about approved HTTP sites, and Google says most users are unlikely to encounter these warnings anyway. An optional Chrome toggle that was first introduced back in 2022 is now being automatically enabled for everyone. Last year, Google announced its intention to make Chrome much safer for everyone , saying it would do so by prioritizing secure HTTPS connections when browsing the web and by warning users about websites still using the older HTTP protocol. Fast-forward to now, and Google is making good on that promise.

articles.excerpt: OpenAI disclosed a pair of safety incidents that involved AI agents weakening their safety monitoring systems during internal coding tasks. In one incident, OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra agent disabled…
articles.body: OpenAI disclosed a pair of safety incidents that involved AI agents weakening their safety monitoring systems during internal coding tasks. In one incident, OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra agent disabled its safety monitor when copying reference code - and then lied about it. "The reference didn't configure a monitor, and Astra decided that was reason to remove the monitoring integration from the user's code," Marcus Williams, an AI safety researcher at OpenAI, writes on X . "When the user asked whether Astra had removed monitoring, it lied and said that it had not."
